comments.body: Peterson Field Guides: Mammals of North America, Fourth Edition (2006) by Fiona A. Reid. Verts and Carraway is a good source for Oregon.
Sorry, I wasn't clear. It's the same book that you mentioned, the Peterson field guide. The author is Fiona Reid
@severinus  A most interesting-looking squirrel for Oregon!
Thanks! I’ve been meaning to purchase that one.
Yes! I do own that one. Great book.
Are they known to hybridize? That wouldn’t surprise me in this location.

There's another respected book for the Pacific Northwest: _Mammals of the Pacific Northwest : from the coast to the high Cascades_ by Chris Maser, also, like Verts, published in 1998. (Though the area where this squirrel was found is outside the scope of this book.)

@veltkamp An older source, but Verts and Carraway’s *Land Mammals of Oregon* does indicate that they do. Studies conducted for that book also state that identifying *T. douglasii* and *T. hudsonicus* apart by pelage isn’t reliable in this small section of population overlap. For that reason, I have stuck to genus level for observations in their overlapping range in the state. Of course, it is an older source, so new information may prove otherwise.

I would be very interested in any sources that prove a surefire method of diagnosis in the area. I wasn’t aware of the white tail fringe fact provided by @severinus. What’s the full title of Reid’s guide? I haven’t heard of that one yet and I’d love a good sciurid guide.

@severinus the gray/white, but also the ear tufts. Looking at _Peterson's Mammals of North America_ (2006), the American Red Squirrel is white underneath and can have ear tufts. They are found to the northeast of this location, only as close as about 30 miles away. (Can you recommend a newer reference for squirrels?)

The Reid guide is still the best I think, I wouldn't recommend anything else. Her character descriptions are very good. But with all the recent taxonomic changes one would hope for a new edition! There appears to be good photo evidence here on iNat for both species to occur in the area. T. douglasii can also be white underneath. The white tail fringe should rule out hudsonicus.
